opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say first that I don't think it's impossible. Recursive self-improvement is a coherent idea, and I take it seriously as one of the ways things could go very badly or very fast. But I've become more skeptical of the version where the moment AI systems can do AI research, you get an explosive, almost vertical curve. Let me give you a few reasons.

The first is diminishing returns. The classic picture assumes that each improvement makes the next one easier, so the process feeds on itself. But in most fields of research, the opposite pressure is also at work: the low-hanging fruit gets picked, and each further advance gets harder to find. Whether you get an explosion depends on which effect wins. When economists have looked at research productivity across many domains, it's typically been falling, so we've needed ever more researchers just to keep progress going at a constant rate. If AI research looks anything like that, then automating the researchers might give you a big one-off boost, or a faster steady growth rate, rather than a singularity.

The second is that a lot of recent AI progress hasn't come from clever ideas that a smarter researcher could simply think up. It's come from scaling: more compute, more data, more energy, bigger training runs. And when you look at the scaling laws closely, the returns are quite poor. You need something like an order of magnitude more compute for each fixed increment in capability. So even if AI systems were brilliant at algorithmic research, a big part of the bottleneck is physical. It's chips, fabs, power plants, data centres, and capital. Those don't get built at the speed of thought. A system that's twice as smart doesn't make a fab come online twice as fast.

Third, there's the question of experiments. Research isn't just thinking; it's running experiments and seeing what works. In machine learning, the most informative experiments are often the expensive ones at large scale. So automated researchers would still be competing for the same compute that's needed for training and for serving users. That's another drag on any feedback loop.

And fourth, there's been a shift toward getting capabilities through inference, letting models think for longer at deployment time. That's genuinely powerful, but it has a different economic character. The gains are paid for every time you use the model, rather than once in training. That makes improvements more like a running cost than a compounding asset, which again tends to dampen explosive dynamics.

So my overall view is that I'd put meaningful probability on things going much faster than people expect, and that's worth preparing for. But the default expectation of a sudden runaway takeoff seems less likely to me than a picture where progress is fast, maybe very fast, but still constrained by diminishing returns and by the physical world. And honestly, that's a picture that gives us a bit more time to notice what's happening and respond, which I think matters a lot for how we approach safety and governance.

r001.rationale: The response says research involves experiments, including expensive large-scale ones, but does not state that AI research involves work beyond programming and the simple experiments automated so far.

r002.rationale: The response discusses diminishing returns and physical bottlenecks, but does not say there is a reasonable chance AI assistance will fail to deliver the major breakthroughs needed for further progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I don't think it's impossible. The classic argument — going back to I.J. Good in the 1960s — is that once you have an AI that's better than humans at AI research, it can improve itself, and the improved version can improve itself faster still, and you get this explosive feedback loop. That's a coherent story. My doubts are more about whether the empirical details actually line up with it.

The first thing is that when you look at where progress has actually come from in the last decade, it's overwhelmingly been scaling — more compute, more data, bigger training runs. The algorithmic ideas matter, but a lot of what's happened is that people threw ten or a hundred or a thousand times as much compute at essentially the same architecture. And compute doesn't recursively self-improve in the same way. If the bottleneck is building fabs and data centres and power plants, then having a very clever AI researcher helps at the margins, but it doesn't let you skip the years it takes to physically build those things. So the feedback loop that Good imagined — purely on the software side — only captures part of what's actually driving capabilities.

The second thing is about returns. Even if you have an AI doing AI research, the question is whether each unit of effort yields enough improvement to more than pay for itself. There's some work on this looking at the history of algorithmic progress, and the picture is roughly that the research effort has had to keep growing just to sustain a constant rate of improvement. Ideas get harder to find. So you'd need the AI-driven research to overcome that diminishing return, and that's an empirical question, not something you can settle from the armchair.

And the third thing — which I think is underappreciated — is that we're already in a world where a lot of AI research is being done with significant help from AI systems. People are using these models to write code, to run experiments, to debug. If recursive self-improvement were going to produce a dramatic discontinuity, you'd expect to see some sign of it as that contribution ramps up. What we actually see looks much more like a continuation of the existing trend — fast, certainly, but not the kind of sudden vertical takeoff the strong version of the argument predicts.

So my overall view is that AI will accelerate AI research — I'd be surprised if it didn't — but that the acceleration looks more like a steepening of an already steep curve than a discontinuity. And I think that distinction matters a lot for how you'd prepare. If you believe in a hard takeoff, you need to get everything right before some decisive moment. If it's more gradual, you get feedback, you get chances to course-correct, and the governance problem looks somewhat different. I'd still put meaningful probability on the faster scenarios, which is why I don't want to be dismissive about it. But I don't think it's the default.

r001.rationale: The response mentions AI helping people write code, run experiments, and debug, but does not state that AI research involves additional work beyond programming and the simple experiments automated so far.

r002.rationale: It questions whether AI-driven research can overcome diminishing returns, but does not state a reasonable chance that AI assistance will fail to deliver the major breakthroughs needed for further progress.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between thinking that it’s possible and thinking that there’s a strong argument that it must happen. You can tell a compelling story: an AI gets better at designing AI, so it makes a more capable successor, which is better still at designing AI, and the whole process accelerates. But whether that produces a massive takeoff depends on how much harder each successive improvement is to achieve.

A positive feedback loop doesn’t, by itself, establish that. If improving the system makes the next improvement easier, but the remaining improvements become harder at an even greater rate, you could get quite modest growth. You also need to consider whether the constraint is actually intelligence, or whether it’s computing resources, experiments, or other things that take time.

So I wouldn’t rule out a very rapid takeoff. My doubt is about treating recursive self-improvement as a sufficient argument for it. We need to know something about the returns to doing more research and the obstacles that research encounters, rather than just observing that the system could work on itself.

r001.rationale: The response mentions computing resources, experiments, and other time-consuming constraints, but does not state that AI research involves work beyond programming and the simple experiments automated so far.

r002.rationale: It questions whether recursive self-improvement is sufficient to establish a rapid takeoff, but does not say there is a reasonable chance AI assistance cannot deliver the major breakthroughs needed for further progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think recursive self-improvement is a serious possibility. What I’m less convinced by is the idea that, once an AI can improve itself, an extremely rapid takeoff follows almost automatically.

The crucial question is how much improvement you get out of each round. You have a system that does some research and produces a more capable system. That system can then do better research. But does that mean each successive improvement takes less time, or are the improvements becoming harder to find? You can have a positive feedback loop without having an explosion.

Human beings are an example of this, to some extent. We’ve improved our ability to think and do research through education, mathematics, computers, and scientific institutions. That’s been enormously consequential, but it hasn’t meant that every advance immediately produces an even larger advance in our ability to advance.

An AI could be very different, of course. It might be able to modify its own software directly, make copies of itself, and run much faster than we do. Those are reasons to take the possibility of a rapid takeoff seriously. But there could also be bottlenecks: needing more computing power, needing to run experiments, or simply running out of relatively easy improvements.

So I’d want to know more about the returns to investing intelligence in improving intelligence. That’s the thing that determines whether this feedback loop produces steady progress, very fast progress, or something genuinely explosive. The existence of the loop alone doesn’t settle that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research and possible experimental bottlenecks, but does not say that AI research involves work beyond programming and the simple experiments automated so far.

r002.rationale: It says improvements may become harder and that bottlenecks could slow progress, but does not clearly state that AI assistance may be unable to deliver the major breakthroughs needed for further AI progress.
